```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  echo     = FALSE )

bench_dir   <- 'benchmark_ord_stats'
timings     <- readRDS(file.path(bench_dir, 'ord_stats_results.rds'))
agreement   <- readRDS(file.path(bench_dir, 'ord_stats_agreement.rds'))
determinism <- readRDS(file.path(bench_dir, 'ord_stats_determinism.rds'))

fmt_time <- function (s)
  ifelse(s < 1e-3, sprintf('%.0f µs', s * 1e6),
  ifelse(s < 1,    sprintf('%.1f ms', s * 1e3),
  ifelse(s < 60,   sprintf('%.2f s',  s),
                   sprintf('%.1f min', s / 60) )))

fmt_bytes <- function (b)
  ifelse(b < 1024^2, sprintf('%.0f KB', b / 1024),
  ifelse(b < 1024^3, sprintf('%.1f MB', b / 1024^2),
                     sprintf('%.2f GB', b / 1024^3) ))

fmt_x <- function (x)
  ifelse(x < 1.5, sprintf('%.1fx', x), formatC(round(x), format = 'd', big.mark = ','))

yes_no <- function (x) ifelse(is.na(x), '—', ifelse(x, 'yes', '**no**'))

gh <- function (path, label = basename(path))
  sprintf('[%s](https://github.com/cmmr/ecodive/blob/main/%s)', label, path)
```


# Introduction

The [alpha and beta diversity benchmarks](benchmark.html) compare ecodive's
diversity metrics with those of 15 other R packages. This page does the same
for the ordination methods and permutation tests: each ecodive function is
timed against the R functions it replaces, on the same data, with ecodive
running on 4 CPU threads.

Speed is worth nothing if the answers are wrong. So this page first sets out
what ecodive claims about its results, and the evidence behind each claim:

1. **Equivalence.** Every function gives the same result as an established
   implementation, to floating-point rounding wherever the method is
   deterministic.
2. **Determinism.** The same call always returns the same result, bit for
   bit, on any number of threads, with or without `set.seed()`.

Both claims are checked twice: by ecodive's test suite, against stored
results from the reference packages, and again below on the benchmark data
itself.


<br>


# Equivalence

### What "the same result" means

The methods fall into three groups, and "the same" means something different
for each.

* **Deterministic methods** (PCoA and its corrections, PCA, db-RDA, capscale,
  envfit, and the test statistics of PERMANOVA, PERMDISP, ANOSIM, MRPP and
  Mantel). There is one right answer, and ecodive returns it: scores,
  eigenvalues and statistics agree with the reference to about 1e-10 or
  better, relative to the largest value. Ordination axes may come out with
  the opposite sign, which carries no meaning, so signs are matched before
  comparing.

* **Permutation p-values.** A p-value depends on which random permutations
  were drawn. Given the *same* permutations as vegan (ecodive's
  `permutations` argument accepts vegan's permutation matrices), ecodive
  computes the same statistic for every one of them, and so the same
  p-value, exactly. With its own permutations, p-values differ from vegan's
  only as much as two vegan runs with different seeds do.

* **Iterative methods with random starts or stochastic steps** (metric MDS,
  NMDS, t-SNE, UMAP). Each start converges to a different, equally valid
  layout, so coordinates can't match any other package's, or even vegan's
  own from another seed. Here ecodive is checked two ways: each algorithm's
  deterministic parts (affinities, neighbour graphs, gradients, steps from a
  shared starting layout) are compared with the reference implementation to
  rounding, and its final layouts are compared on quality measures (stress,
  KL divergence, neighbours kept), on which ecodive must do at least as well.

### Evidence from the test suite

Each test below compares ecodive with results stored from the reference
package, so the tests need no reference package installed. The scripts in
`r gh('data-raw/expected', 'data-raw/expected/')` produce those results, and the tests in
`r gh('tests/tinytests', 'tests/tinytests/')` run on GitHub CI on Linux, macOS and Windows.
Tolerances are relative differences.

| Function | Reference | What is compared | Tolerance | Test |
|:---------|:----------|:-----------------|:----------|:-----|
| `pcoa()` | `stats::cmdscale()`, `ape::pcoa()`, `vegan::wcmdscale()` | Scores (up to sign), eigenvalues, proportions, total inertia | 1e-9 scores; 1e-10 the rest | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-pcoa.r', 'test-pcoa.r')` |
| `pcoa(correction =)` | `ape::pcoa()`, `vegan::wcmdscale()`, `cmdscale(add = TRUE)` | Lingoes and Cailliez constants, corrected eigenvalues, scores | 1e-10; 1e-8 scores | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-pcoa_correct.r', 'test-pcoa_correct.r')` |
| `pcoa_biplot()` | scikit-bio 0.7.4 | Eigenvalues, coordinates, biplot scores | 1e-12; 1e-10 scores | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-pcoa_biplot.r', 'test-pcoa_biplot.r')` |
| `mds()` | scikit-learn 1.9.1 (SMACOF) | From the same start: iteration count (exact), stress at every 10th iteration, final layout. Quality: stress no worse than scikit-learn's best | 1e-10 stress; 1e-8 layout | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-mds.r', 'test-mds.r')` |
| `nmds()` | scikit-learn 1.9.1; `vegan::metaMDS()` | As `mds()`; and stress no worse than vegan's | 1e-10 stress; 1e-8 layout | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-nmds.r', 'test-nmds.r')` |
| `isomap()` | scikit-learn 1.9.1 | Neighbour graph (exact), geodesic distances, embedding, eigenvalues | 1e-12 geodesics; 1e-9 embedding | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-isomap.r', 'test-isomap.r')` |
| `tsne()` | scikit-learn 1.9.1; `Rtsne::Rtsne()` | Affinities; exact and Barnes-Hut KL divergence and gradients; the first iterations' steps. Quality: KL, trustworthiness and nearest-neighbour accuracy over 10 seeds | 1e-10 exact; 1e-6 where scikit-learn uses single precision | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-tsne.r', 'test-tsne.r')` |
| `umap()` | `uwot::umap(batch = TRUE)` 0.2.5 | Nearest neighbours and fuzzy graph (exact), curve parameters, spectral start, optimised layout from the same start and seeds | 1e-14 graph; 0 (bit-identical) layout on Windows x86_64 | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-umap.r', 'test-umap.r')` |
| `dbrda()` | `vegan::dbrda()` | Site scores, eigenvalues, inertia, R², adjusted R², biplot scores, centroids | 1e-10 | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-dbrda.r', 'test-dbrda.r')` |
| `capscale()` | `vegan::capscale()` | As `dbrda()`, plus imaginary inertia | 1e-10 | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-capscale.r', 'test-capscale.r')` |
| `pca()` | `stats::prcomp()` | Scores and loadings (up to sign), eigenvalues, proportions | 1e-10 | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-pca.r', 'test-pca.r')` |
| `rpca()` | gemelli 0.0.13 (Python) | Every stage: rclr, starting subspaces, cost per iteration, completed matrix; final scores, loadings and distances | 1e-10 | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-rpca.r', 'test-rpca.r')` |
| `envfit()` | `vegan::envfit()` | Arrows, r², centroids; p-values with vegan's permutations | 1e-10; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-envfit.r', 'test-envfit.r')` |
| `permanova()` | `vegan::adonis2()` | The whole table (Df, SS, R², F); every permuted F; p-values | 1e-10; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-permanova.r', 'test-permanova.r')` |
| `permdisp()` | `vegan::betadisper()`, `vegan::permutest()` | Distances to centres, dispersions, ANOVA table, every permuted F, p-values | 1e-10; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-permdisp.r', 'test-permdisp.r')` |
| `anosim()` | `vegan::anosim()` | R, every permuted R, mean ranks, p-values | 1e-14; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-anosim.r', 'test-anosim.r')` |
| `mrpp()` | `vegan::mrpp()` | δ, expected δ, A, every permuted δ, z, p-values | 1e-12; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-mrpp.r', 'test-mrpp.r')` |
| `mantel()` | `vegan::mantel()`, `vegan::mantel.partial()` | r (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall; partial), every permuted r, p-values | 1e-12; p-values identical | `r gh('tests/tinytests/test-mantel.r', 'test-mantel.r')` |

### Where ecodive deliberately differs

* **`permdisp(type = 'median')`.** vegan finds each group's spatial median
  with a general-purpose optimiser that stops early, so its medians are only
  accurate to about 1e-5. ecodive solves for the exact median, and its
  results agree with an exact solution to 1e-10, and with vegan's to about
  1e-3. The default, `type = 'centroid'`, has no such difference.
* **`umap()`** always uses uwot's batch optimiser (`batch = TRUE`), which can
  run in parallel and still give the same layout every time. uwot's default
  optimiser can't do both. Its `min_dist` default is 0.1, as in Python's
  umap-learn (uwot's is 0.01).
* **`tsne()`** follows scikit-learn but computes in double precision
  throughout, where scikit-learn uses single precision for parts of the
  calculation. It starts from PCoA by default.
* **`nmds()` and `mds()`** start from PCoA plus random starts and take
  relaxed (faster) SMACOF steps. They reproduce scikit-learn's iterations
  exactly only when given its start and plain steps, which is how the tests
  check them.
* **`dbrda()`** reproduces `vegan::dbrda()`, and **`capscale()`**
  reproduces `vegan::capscale()`. The two differ for non-Euclidean
  distances, in vegan as in ecodive.
* A few edge cases are handled differently: for example, `envfit()` gives
  `NA` rather than 1 as the p-value of a constant variable, and `pcoa()`
  drops axes with non-positive eigenvalues instead of returning columns of
  zeros.

### Evidence from the benchmark data

The same comparisons, repeated on the benchmark data set (1,006 samples; see
[Setup](#setup)). "Relative difference" is the largest absolute difference
divided by the largest absolute value in the reference result. For the
permutation tests, ecodive and vegan were both given the same 999
permutations.

```{r}
tbl <- agreement
tbl$value <- ifelse(
  grepl('^[0-9.e+-]+$', tbl$value),
  sprintf('%s (relative difference)', tbl$value),
  tbl$value )
names(tbl) <- c('Method', 'Reference', 'Quantity', 'Agreement')
knitr::kable(tbl, row.names = FALSE)
```


<br>


# Determinism

ecodive's results depend only on the inputs and the `seed` argument. They
never depend on:

* **The number of threads.** Work is split into the same pieces whatever
  `cpus` is, and each piece is summed in a fixed order, so the floating-point
  rounding never changes.
* **R's random number generator.** Methods with random parts take a `seed`
  argument (default `0`) and use their own generator. Calling the same
  function twice gives the same result, without `set.seed()`, and ecodive
  never changes R's random state.
* **Timing.** Threads never race to update shared values.

That matters for reproducible research: a p-value or a plot from a paper can
be regenerated exactly, on a laptop or on a 64-core server.

Many R packages are deterministic only after `set.seed()`, and some not even
then once they use more than one thread. Each function below was run five
times with its default arguments: twice in a row; twice more, each after
`set.seed(1)`; and once more after `set.seed(1)` with one thread instead of
four. A "yes" means the results were bit-for-bit identical.

```{r}
tbl <- determinism
tbl$rerun            <- yes_no(tbl$rerun)
tbl$rerun_same_seed  <- yes_no(tbl$rerun_same_seed)
tbl$one_vs_4_threads <- yes_no(tbl$one_vs_4_threads)
tbl <- tbl[order(tbl$package != 'ecodive', tbl$package), ]
names(tbl) <- c('Method', 'Package', 'Run twice', 'Run twice after `set.seed(1)`', '1 vs 4 threads')
knitr::kable(tbl, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Speed

### Methodology

The `bench` R package timed each function and measured the memory it
allocated on R's heap. All benchmarks ran on:

    CPU: 6-Core Intel i5-9600K @ 3.70GHz
    RAM: 64.0 GB
    OS:  Windows 11 Pro (64-bit, Build 26300)
    R:   4.6.1, with R's reference BLAS

ecodive used 4 threads (`cpus = 4`). Every other package that can use
several threads was given 4 as well: `Rtsne` (`num_threads`), `uwot`
(`n_threads`, `n_sgd_threads`), and vegan's permutation tests and NMDS
(`parallel = 4`). On Windows, vegan's `parallel` starts a cluster of R
processes on every call, which can make it slower than running serially, so
vegan's tests were timed both ways.

A few things to keep in mind:

* Other packages' eigendecompositions (`cmdscale()`, `prcomp()`, vegan's
  constrained ordinations) call BLAS and LAPACK. With an optimised,
  multithreaded BLAS such as OpenBLAS or Intel MKL, they would run faster
  than with R's reference BLAS used here. ecodive computes only the few axes
  that are returned, in its own threaded C, so its speed hardly depends on
  the BLAS.
* `bench` counts only memory allocated on R's heap. That covers most of what
  these functions allocate, ecodive's included, but not memory that C or
  Fortran code allocates directly.
* Where packages have different defaults, they were set to do comparable
  work: four starts for each NMDS and MDS that supports several, 999
  permutations for every test, and three axes for PCoA and PCA. The
  iterative methods then stop when their own convergence criteria are met.

<a id="setup"></a>

### Setup

The `gems` data set from the `rbiom` package has 1,006 stool samples from
children in four countries, with 767 OTUs, each sample's diarrhea status
(case or control), age, and country. The benchmarks use its Bray-Curtis
distances, which every method takes as its input, except PCA, which takes
centered log-ratio transformed counts. The tests ask whether country explains
the distances, and the Mantel test correlates them with differences in age.
Distances and other inputs are computed before the timed code.

```{r}
tbl <- timings
tbl <- tbl[order(match(tbl$method, unique(tbl$method)), tbl$seconds), ]
tbl <- data.frame(
  Method            = ifelse(duplicated(tbl$method), '', tbl$method),
  Package           = ifelse(tbl$package == 'ecodive', '**ecodive**', tbl$package),
  `Median time`     = fmt_time(tbl$seconds),
  `Times slower`    = ifelse(tbl$package == 'ecodive', '', fmt_x(tbl$speedup)),
  `Memory (R heap)` = fmt_bytes(tbl$bytes),
  check.names = FALSE )
knitr::kable(tbl, row.names = FALSE, align = 'llrrr')
```
